title: Two calls at once
stem:
You are an F2 doctor covering paediatrics overnight. A nurse on the children's ward tells you that Ben, 6, who has pneumonia, has a tissued cannula with maintenance fluids running through it, and his next dose of IV antibiotics is due in 30 minutes.

At the same moment, a midwife bleeps you to see a newborn on the postnatal ward who is grunting and has oxygen saturations of 89%.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Ask a colleague who is free whether they could re-site Ben's cannula.
options.brief: Gets Ben's cannula sorted without delaying the newborn.
options.detailed: Another doctor may be able to help with the cannula. It ranks second because the newborn's assessment comes first.

options.text: Ask Ben's nurse to stop the infusion, and let her know when you expect to be back.
options.brief: Keeps the nurse informed and prevents further tissuing.
options.detailed: Stopping the infusion prevents further harm to the tissue, and telling the nurse your plan helps her manage Ben and his parents.

options.brief: A grunting baby with low saturations may be seriously unwell.
options.detailed: Grunting and low saturations in a newborn can be signs of respiratory distress or infection, which need urgent assessment. Ben's antibiotics can wait a short time.

options.text: Re-site Ben's cannula first, as it will only take a few minutes.
options.brief: Cannulating a child can take longer than expected, and the newborn may be unwell.
options.detailed: Cannulas in children are often difficult and can take much longer than planned, delaying the assessment of a newborn who may be seriously unwell. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Ask the nurse to give Ben's next dose orally instead.
options.brief: Changing the route of an antibiotic needs assessment.
options.detailed: Switching to oral antibiotics may be appropriate later, but it's a clinical decision that needs review, not a solution to a cannula problem.

explanation.issue: This tests how you prioritise two calls and use colleagues to keep both patients safe.
explanation.keyDetails: The newborn may be seriously unwell. Ben's antibiotics are due in 30 minutes. Other doctors may be available.
explanation.reasoning: [C] sees the sickest patient first, [A] gets help for Ben, and [B] keeps the nurse informed. [E] changes treatment without assessment, and [D] delays the newborn.
explanation.competing: The order of [A] and [B] is close. The key puts getting help first because it solves Ben's problem, whereas updating the nurse only manages it. [D] ranks last because delaying a possibly sick newborn carries the greatest risk.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, prioritising patients according to clinical need.
